title: People Who Didn't Receive Praise as Children
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership identifies a distinct personality type on teams: people who grew up without receiving much praise and as adults find compliments uncomfortable, disingenuous, or simply irrelevant to their internal accounting system. These team members do not reject praise out of false modesty — they genuinely learned to depend on internal rather than external validation, so general praise doesn't register as psychologically rewarding. The article identifies 'observational praise' as the workaround: specific, behaviorally detailed recognition that can be cross-checked against the person's own internal standards and thus actually lands. The piece ends with the advice that making specific observation a habit for all team members, not just praise-averse ones, produces stronger recognition across the board.
points: People who grew up without much praise often perceive adult compliments as disingenuous influence attempts or irrelevant noise — not false modesty, but a genuinely different validation architecture built in childhood.
Because praise strengthens social bonds and signals inclusion, leaders cannot simply ignore these team members' needs; they need an alternative pathway that bypasses the rejection reflex.

Observational praise works because specificity contains data: 'You patiently listened to me when I was agitated' can be cross-checked against the person's internal accounting system, and when it matches, the recognition lands like it would for anyone else.
The practical swap: replace 'Great job' with 'You caught the error before it became a bigger problem'; replace 'You're so smart' with 'You connected those two ideas quickly.'

Observation-based recognition is a universally superior recognition habit — it works better for all team members, not just the praise-averse, because it signals that the leader is paying genuine attention.
quotes: People who grew up without receiving much praise have an unusual affliction. They often struggle with compliments as adults. Strangely enough, compliments and praise create real discomfort for them. This isn't false modesty. They often perceive praise and compliments as disingenuous attempts to influence them. Or as superfluous noise.

They learned as children to depend on their own internal validation, praise directed at them doesn't register as psychologically rewarding, as it does for other adults. Unless it perfectly matches their own internal accounting, praise and compliments are viewed as words without much value.

The best way to encourage a praise-allergic team member isn't through general praise or enthusiastic compliments. It's through observation. Observational praise and compliments cut through the noise and positively influence these team members in the same way general praise works with everyone else.

'You did an amazing job' doesn't register, but 'You patiently listened to me when I was agitated' does. The more specific the observation, the better. Specificity contains data that can be cross-checked and run through their internal validation system.
Observation of praise-worthy behavior lands well with all team members, not just those who view praise as uncomfortable and unnecessary.
